MO009-051----:
Situated on top of a broad hill. This is a gallery (L 2.5m) orientated NNW-SSE with two E side stones and a large S back stone. A low stone at right angles to E side of the gallery may be buttress. It remains unclassified but it is probably a wedge-tomb.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

MO009-063----:
Located on the crest of a hill in a forested area with commanding views of the Twin Lakes to the S. The remains consist of four deeply set orthostats, aligned E-W, and a large boulder-like capstone 0.2m to the N. The capstone rises to a height of c. 0.5m above the surrounding ground level and there is a small cavity c. 0.25m deep underneath it. No evidence of a cairn survives. (CRDS 1998, 33)
Date of upload: 14 April 2011
MO012-028----:
Situated towards the bottom of a W-facing slope. This is the remains of a back-to-back dual court-tomb, orientated approximately NE-SW, which is incorporated in a field bank. A single court stone and an entry jamb of the NE tomb survive. The gallery (L 5.5m; Wth 1.6m), narrowing towards the rear, is divided into two chambers by two jamb -stones. Two jamb-stones, a single side-stone, and the adjoining shared back stone are all that survive of the SW gallery. There are indeterminate remains of a cairn (diam. 8m). (de Valera 1960, 123)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 17 July 2007
MO012-030----:
Located on a slight shelf of a SE-facing slope. This is a grass and scrub-covered trapezoidal cairn (L 40m; Wth 23m at E) orientated ENE-WSW. Six stones to the N and two to the S define the extent of a broad, probable three-quarter court (Wth 9m) at its E end. To the N and S of the court and about 1-2m E of it are two large blocks, perhaps vestiges of the façade. The gallery entrance and adjoining court stones are apparently covered by the cairn. The gallery has three stones; a N side-stone and jamb-stone of the chamber and to the W, the S side-stone of the adjoining, inner chamber. A single subsidiary chamber opens to the W at the rear of cairn. To the S of this is a set block which may mark the back of the cairn. A portion of a drystone kerb (L 3m) survives along the SW edge of the cairn. (de Valera 1960, 123)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload: 17 July 2007

MO012-041----:
Located on rock outcrop towards the bottom of the SE-facing slope of the spine of a NW-SE drumlin ridge. It is marked only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map where it is described in gothic lettering as ‘Cairnbaine Giant’s Grave’. This is probably a dual court-tomb incorporated into a trapezoidal cairn aligned ENE-WSW (L 36m; max. Wth 19m at E). The E tomb has the remains of a three-quarter court (L 6.5m; Wth 5.5m) with two façade stones to the N of the gallery. Two entry jambs surmounted by a lintel give access to a chamber (L 4m; Wth 1.7m). Beyond this, two segmenting jambs indicate a continuation of the gallery. At the opposite end of the cairn is a chamber (L 2.3m; Wth 1.2m) with double jambs open to the W. (de Valera 1960, 123).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
This is a National Monument in Guardianship: No. 367

MO012-048----:
Situated in a slight col on top of an ENE-WSW drumlin ridge with slightly higher ground to the E and WSW. This is a court-tomb comprising a long cairn (L 30m; max. Wth 9m) aligned WNW-ESE. Incorporated in the cairn 15m from the W end are the remains of a gallery (L c. 9m; Wth 1.2m) divided into two chambers by segmenting jambs. Entry jambs at the W are doubled; the front pair are exceptionally large and well matched. The easternmost stone in the gallery, partly set inside the line of the chamber, may indicate further segmentation. Three kerb stones survive N of the gallery.

MO012-065----:
Located at the crest of the S-facing slope of a hill that is known as Fall Crom. The hill is thought to have been an inauguration site of a branch of Ó Mórdha of Laois (Moore) who migrated here during the seventeenth century (Moore 2014). The stone is represented only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map as ‘Ancient Stone (Site of)’. It was described in 1941 (SMR file) as ‘two upright stones 3 feet high (c. 0.9m) remain in the hedge. Two or three others were removed some time ago….. The stones apparently formed a small ring.’ No stones are present now, although a lot of field stones are in the field bank just to the N.

MO012-078----:
Located towards the SE end of a narrow E-W ridge or spur, overlooking Anagose Lough to the SW, and to the N there is a small ESE-WNW valley opening out to the W. A small chamber (L 1.9m; Wth 0.9m) defined by three side stones and a transversely set stone, perhaps indicating a portico, is aligned E-W. Two roof stones suggest a gallery extending 3m to the E. Two stones to the N of the chamber entrance may be façade stones; three others, one beneath the easternmost roof stone, may represent outer walling. The structure is incorporated in a cairn (L 7m; Wth 5m) and partly concealed by a field bank at SW. It is probably a wedge-tomb.

MO012-080----:
Located towards the top of a S-facing slope and just below a col with higher ground c. 200m to the NW and c. 300m to the NE. From the descriptions available there is little doubt that this was a megalithic tomb of the court-tomb class. It was described in 1841 in newspaper reports quoted by Borlase (1897, 291-3) as being a hillock in a small meadow close to a farmhouse from which several spits of turf had been removed. The outer wall of the cairn was distinct and measured 46 feet by 16 feet (c. 14m x c. 5m). It was not depicted on any edition of the OS 6-inch map, and the location could have been lost forever. The tomb had been removed by the 1940s and was not even remembered locally. However, the schoolmaster identified the location for Oliver Davies as a place where people knew of the former existence of ‘tunnels’ (SMR file). The original description by Rev. T. Stopford is worth quoting extensively:
‘Outside the entrance is a semi-circular courtyard. The base of the wall surrounding it, as well as that of all the other walls, is composed of large rough stones, some of them several tons weight, standing on the ends, something like those of Stonehenge.
The entrance divided the semi-circular wall into two equal segments, and was formed with two larger stones than the others, sufficiently apart to admit a man with ease. Inside the entrance was an oval apartment about 12 feet by 8 feet (c. 3.65m x c. 2.4m), which was arched over from within c. 4 feet (c, 1.2m) of the base. The arch was composed of flat stones of different sizes, so carefully selected and fitted.. that the point of a penknife could scarcely be inserted between them. Each stone projected from the underneath one, until they met at the top of the roof, which was about six feet (c. 1.8m) from the ground.
Opposite the entrance, at the other end of his room was a similar entrance into a lobby, which led straight to the other extremity of the building, and off which were six other apartments, all square, and built and roofed in the same manner as the first oval one. Two standing stones forming the entrance from this latter room into the corridor stood somewhat narrower than those of the principal entrance, and were rubbed and worn on one particular part, as it were from the weapons of the inhabitants, returning from their hunting or plundering excursions.
The whole of the floor inside was flagged with slabs of the same stone, and the outside of the roof covered with the same material, which is the most remarkable circumstance connected with it as (it is freestone) and the nearest freestone quarry is on Carrowmore Mountain, in the county of Fermanagh, about twenty miles from this place, and the stone there doesn’t cleave into slabs, and is of quite different grain, the former (i.e. the stone of which the floor and roof of the chamber is built) exactly resembling the Scotch sandstone found along the Clyde.
The interior was found to be perfectly clean, except that the juice of the bog stuff covered it, having trickled down the walls. …
MO012-081----:
Located on a broad E-W spur and incorporated in a kink of a NW-SE field bank on the SW side. A chamber (L 2m; Wth 1m), opening to the NNW, is represented by two portal stones, two side stones on either side, and a back stone. The roof stone is displaced and leaning against one of the E side-stones. It is listed as a portal tomb (Ó Nualláin 1983, 100), and is a nearly perfect example of one.

MO012-083----:
Located on a slight rise in a broad W-facing valley with the headwaters of a small E-W stream immediately to the S. This was a dual court tomb that was removed between 1857 and 1907. A plan of the monument among OS records shows two very similar two-chambered galleries aligned N-S and set 4m apart, back to back: N chamber (L 4m), S chamber (L 4.4m). Two set and three displaced stones surviving along the S side of an E-W road fence appear to represent the remains of a court. (Ó Nualláin 1977)

MO012-094----:
This tomb, discovered in 2011 (pers. comm. Emmett Connolly 11th May 2011), is situated on top of a low drumlin in undulating pasture land. It stands at the W end of an abandoned farmstead and an out-building has been built at its E end. As part of a working farm over many generations (the buildings are represented on the OS 1st ed. map) the monument has suffered accordingly. It was planted with conifers and its E end incorporated in a stone field boundary: the remnants of older boundaries abut the NW and SE ends of the monument. The presence of modern dry-stone walling in the subsidiary chamber to the S of the monument suggests that this may have been used as a possible animal pen or storage area.
The remains consist of a long cairn measuring at least 30m in length and approximately 13m wide. Three substantial upright stones indicate a U-shaped court at the W; it is c. 7m long by at least 6.5m wide. At the E end of the court two well-matched jambs (see MO012-094----_03.jpg) give access to the gallery, 6.7m long by 1.8m in maximum width, represented by four sidestones at the N and two at the S with a low inset backstone closing its E end . There is no evident segmentation of the gallery though, given its length, it is likely to have had two chambers. Three upright stones are all that remain of a subsidiary chamber that opens off the S side of the cairn beyond the galley. A substantial orthostat standing beside the corner of the out-building at the NE end of the cairn may mark the location of another subsidiary chamber. Little survives of the cairn at the E end of the monument where the stones were incorporated into field boundaries. Seven contiguous stones form a line of revetment along the N side of the cairn which, if the surviving stones of the S subsidiary chamber represent its original extent, then this would give an overall cairn width at this point of 11m.

Located in woodland on a N-facing slope overlooking Barn Hill Lough which is c. 130m to the NW at the nearest point. There is a shallow court at E consisting of two stones, one on either side of the entry jambs. The chamber (L 3.7m; Wth 1.1m) is aligned E-W and its sides are represented by a single stone to the S and two stones on the N side. A transversely set stone to the W probably indicates segmentation of the gallery. Three large flags 4m N of chamber may be the remains of a kerb.

A megalithic structure consisting of six upright stones (H c. 0.7-1.15m) was first recorded by Oliver Davies in 1942 (SMR file), but no pattern was discerned. There were other prone stones that were probably field stones, and two smaller stones were set in the ground c. 2m to the E. The stones were removed between 1968 and 1984.

Located at the S summit of a N-S drumlin ridge. It is not recorded on any map but is mentioned in the Schools’ Manuscripts (IFC, Schools’ Mss (953) 375: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes ). This is a cairn (L 23m; Wth 11m) orientated NE-SW, incorporating at the NE end the fairly full remains of a three-quarter court (Wth 5.5m NW-SE; D 6m NE-SW). Single façade stones (H 1.1m) survive at either side of the court. A NNE-SSW field boundary crosses the cairn and partly defines the NW extent of the court. The gallery (L 7.2m; Wth 1.5m) narrows from the front to the rear and is divided into three chambers by two sets of jambs.

MO013-029----:
Situated on top of a drumlin. It is well-known in the folk tradition (IFC: (949) 344-5, 482-3; (950) 496-7: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes ), and although no name is associated with it two rather similar and very accurate sketch plans are provided by this sourece. A grass-covered trapezoidal cairn (dims 35m NE-SW; 22m NW-SE at NE) incorporates a deep U-shaped court (Wth 6.5m; D 6.5m) at the broader NE end. Two stones, one at either side of the court are probably façade stones. The court gives access to a gallery (L 9.3m; Wth 1.5m) divided by jambs into three chambers, the end chamber being represented by a single jambstone and the backstone. A fallen lintel lies inside the entrance to the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1977, 52-60)

Located on top of a small drumlin. OS Memoirs record that 'two enormous boulders forming a portion of a Giant's grave, still represent the monument of the Bard' (RIA, Box 49, Aghabog Parish, p.8). This may be the 'cromlech' which was known locally as Fir Breaga – false men, and referred to by O'Donovan writing in the 1830s (P 132) (Herity 2012, 198). The location was identified by Oliver Davies in the 1940s (SMR file) where a number of large stones were extant at the meeting point of three fields and where some large boulders are incorporated into the field boundaries.

Situated on a hilltop. A gallery (L 4.8m; average Wth 0.8m) consisting of a short portico at the W end and a longer main chamber is incorporated in a mound (L 18m; Wth 12m). Outer walling is represented at SE and along the NW of the gallery. Two stones to the N of the outer walling and a single stone to the E of the gallery are probably kerb stones. There is a large stone c. 6m S of the gallery and inside the line of mound, but its function is unclear. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 131)

There are some exposed blocks near the SE end, but no pattern can be discerned. It was listed by de Valera as a possible court-tomb in 1951 (p. 196) but excluded from his list in 1960.

Situated on a slight S-N spur in a low-lying landscape. It is depicted as a circular enclosure (diam. c. 25m E-W) on the 1834 edition of the OS 6-inch map where it is described in gothic lettering as a ‘fort’, and it is represented as rough ground on the 1907 edition. This is an overgrown subrectangular cairn (dims 24m NW-SE; 18m NE-SW) with the remains of a broad court (Wth 6.5m; D 5m) at the SE end. The court gives access through two portal stones to the scant remains of a chamber (L 1.7m; Wth 1.1), but a hollow in the cairn behind it suggests that other chambers have been robbed.

MO014-037----:
Situated towards the SE end of a small NW-SE ridge in a grass-covered area with some rock outcrop and trees. It is depicted as a circular feature described in gothic lettering as a ‘fort’ on the 1834 edition of the OS 6-inch map and as a small copse on the 1907 edition. The monument consists of seven separate chambers in an area (dims c. 30m NW-SE; c. 12m NE-SW). There are two pairs of back-to-back chambers at the SE end, two chambers opening to the SW and two to the NE. A NNW-SSE farm laneway separates these from three chambers to the NW. Immediately to the W of the laneway, a chamber opens to the SW. Behind it are three upright slabs and one fallen. Two chambers at the NW end have opposed entrances facing each other, 2.8m apart. The seven chambers are clearly comparable to the subsidiary chambers found in court-tombs and hence the monument is assigned to this class, although there is no evidence of a court at either end.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

It is described as a ‘Druid’s Circle’ in gothic lettering on the 1834 edition of the OS 6-inch map, and as the site of a ‘Cromlech’ on the 1907 edition. Ordinance Survey Memoirs record 'the partial remains of a Druidical Circle the extent of which cannot be traced' (RIA Box 49, Muckno Parish, 16), and Shirley (1879, 515) describes them as ‘some standing-stones’. No archaeological feature is visible at ground level in pasture.

MO015-007----:
Located in a small clearing on top of and around the middle of the N-S ridge of Mullyash Mountain. Folklore associates it with a princess who unfortunately died in a battle between her husband and her father (IFC: Schools Manuscripts (942) 353-4: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes ), and the cairn was also a centre for Lughnasa celebrations (MacNeill 1962, 161-3). This is a circular cairn (diam. of base 16m; H c. 2.5m) with a kerb of battered drystone walling (at N: H 2m) NNW-E-S but the edge of the original cairn is obscured by collapse elsewhere, and cairn material has spilled over the wall all around. Immediately W of the centre is a modern depression (diam. 3m; D 0.5m). A second inner tier of drystone kerbing is intermittently visible on the summit and there might be an entrance obscured in the cairn at W (Desmond 2000). According to Shirley (1879, 513) 'a cairn was opened … in 1816 and human bones and an earthen bowl were found' at Knocknaneen. As no known cairn exists now in Knocknaneen townland, which is the townland immediately to the N, this may refer to the Mullyash/Tavanaskea cairn. A standing stone (MO020-029----) c. 850m to the SSW in Tavanskea townland was associated with it in the Lughnasa celebrations, but the stone is now lying prone in forestry.
This is a National Monument in state guardianship (NO. 564) accessed by forestry roads, and it is on the Monaghan Way, a sign-posted walking route, for which see this web-page accessed on 13/02/2018: http://blackwaterregion.com/to-do/walking/monaghan-way-walk/
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 26 February 2018

Revised by: Michael Moore

MO017-068----:
Situated on a NE-facing slope on one of the summits on an ENE-WSW drumlin ridge. Three stones in a line ENE-WSW are incorporated in a field bank and are known as the ‘Grey stones’. A fourth stone 5m to the S, has a similar orientation.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 9 May 2018
MO018-012----:
Located on the N bank of an E-W section of a stream, which is immediately to the S and runs through rock outcrop immediately to the W. It is described as a ‘Cromlech’ only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map. It consists of an overgrown chamber aligned NW-SW with a large capstone but there is no visible evidence of a cairn.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 18 June 2018
MO018-043----:
Located at the bottom of the W-facing slope of a knoll on the crest of an E-W drumlin ridge, and incorporated into the N bank of an E-W road. At ENE, two jambs surmounted by a large lintel give access to gallery (L 7.5m; Wth 1.8m). (Borlase 1897, vol. 1, 294; de Valera 1960, 123-4)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

MO018-047----:
Located towards the E end of an E-W drumlin ridge.  The standing stone is marked only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map. The stone (L 2.55m Wth 0.3-0.8m; T 0.55m at wide base; T 1m at centre; T 0.2-0.25m at top) is now prostrate and tapers to a rough point at one end.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 19 June 2018
MO019-010----:
Situated on the W-facing slope of a small N-S ridge. It is marked only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map where it is described in gothic lettering as a ‘Giant’s Grave’. Trees have been planted in the area and there is no evidence of a megalithic structure.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO019-016----:
Located on the SE-facing spine of a small NW-SE drumlin ridge. It is depicted only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map where it is described in gothic lettering as a ‘Cromlech’.  It was built into the outer (SW) edge of a field bank at the SW angle of a field. The roofstone had been dislodged and the western side-stone damaged in 1847, but a scribbing at the edge of a fissure on the damaged side-stone was recorded by John O’Donovan in 1835 (Herity 2012, 182) and Graves in 1848 (Ferguson 1873). This appears to be more like runes than ogham or any other script, but the present condition of the carving is not known. The field bank had been removed by 1983 when the monument was described as a large roofstone (dims 3.4m x 2.6m; T 0.7m) supported on two side-stones (Ó Nualláin 1983, 100). (Borlase 1897 vol. 1, 294)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
See the attached view from Borlase _1, and drawings of the inscription by O'Donovan (above) and Ferguson after Borlase _2
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO019-021----:
Situated on a slight rise in a low-lying landscape between drumlins with a small pot lough (diam. c. 100m) c. 150m to the E. It is depicted only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map where it is described in gothic lettering as a ‘Giants Grave’.  Two orthostats support a lintel, which could be interpreted as the entrance to a court tomb (de Valera 1960, 131).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO019-025----:
Situated on the E-facing spine of an E-W drumlin ridge. From a plan by H. G. Tempest made in 1936 (SMR file) this appears to be a wedge-tomb consisting of gallery aligned NE-SW, flanked by two buttresses and a single outer walling stone on the NW side. The gallery (L 3m; Wth 0.7m) has a short portico at SW. Two displaced roof stones lie across the gallery. The structure is incorporated in a mound (L 11m; Wth 5m). It is listed as a wedge tomb (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 131).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO019-027----:
Situated on a SW-facing slope c. 100m S of a small col between slight rises to the E and W. From a survey by H. G. Tempest made in 1936 (SMR file) it appears to be a cairn (L 28m; Wth 12m) aligned NNE-SSW incorporating a portal-tomb opening to the NNE at the N end. The tomb (L 2m; Wth 1.1m) is represented by pair of portal stones, two side stones, a back stone and a displaced roof stone. The remains of two subsidiary chambers open off the cairn on the E side. It may have been removed since 1984.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO019-030----:
Situated on a NW-facing slope overlooking a slight col. It is represented on the 1834 and 1907 editions of the OS 6-inch map where it is described in gothic lettering as a ‘Giant’s Grave’. A cairn (L 16m; Wth 13m) is aligned NW-SE with a court at the SE end represented by two stones and entry jambs which give access to gallery (L 6.5m; Wth 1.5m) divided by two pairs of jambs into three chambers. According to the local folk record this monument was investigated more than once (IFC: Schools MSS (936) 152-4), for which see this web-page accessed on 29/05/2018: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes  (Borlase 1897 vol. 1, 295; de Valera 1960, 124)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO019-037----:
Situated in a slight col between local summits c. 120m to the N and c. 340m to the SE in an undulating landscape. It is marked on the 1834 and 1907 editions of the OS 6-inch map where it is described in gothic lettering as ‘The Cashel’ and it is now in a small triangular coniferous plantation. It is probably a court-tomb with a roughly trapezoidal cairn (L 29m N-S; Wth 18m) incorporating at the N end a deep U-shaped court (L 6.5m; Wth 3.6m). The gallery is represented by a single side stone.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO019-041----:
Situated on a NE-facing slope. The OS Name Book (1835, Clontibret Parish, No. 143, p. 16) describes this monument as 'oblong stones set upright similar to the Cashel described in page 15' (the court-tomb: MO019-037----). 'The White Stones' are depicted on the OS Fair Plan as a semi-circle of stones with three others tangentially placed at the middle of the curve. There is now no visible evidence of archaeological features in pasture.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 22 June 2018
MO020-029----:
Situated in dense forestry towards the top of a S-facing slope on Mullyash Mountain. The stone is broken into two pieces (piece 1: L c. 2.2m; Wth 2.2m; T at N end 0.6m; piece 2: L c. 0.65m; Wth 0.85m; T 0.6m), and is now recumbent with a flat face of the stone visible. The stone is tapered at both ends and modern graffiti are on the upper face. The stone had a role in the Lughnasa celebrations centred on the passage tomb (MO015-007----), which is on the summit of the ridge c. 850m to the NNW (MacNeill 1962, 161-3). A long stone in Mullyash Plantation 'that had the footprint of a giant marked on it’ was noted in folk tradition (IFC Schools MSS: (942) 158; (943) 274), for which see this web-page accessed on 11/06/2018: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes  Such a mark is not visible on the upper surfaces now. The folk tradition also recorded that Fionn MacCumhaill threw it the length of a field (ibid. 943, 274).
Compiled by: Claire Breen
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revised upload: 22 June 2017
MO024-001----:
Situated on an E-facing slope. It is described in gothic lettering as a ‘Giant’s Grave’ on the 1834 and 1907 editions of the OS 6-inch map. OS Memoirs describe this as 'large stones standing in the form of a rectangle 7 ft. by 3 and a half ft. (dims c. 2.1m x c. 1.05m). Some of these stones are 3 and a half ft. (c. 1.05m) above the surface of the ground' (RIA Box 49, Ballybay Parish, p.14). No detailed description is known and no archaeological feature is visible at ground level in pasture.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 9 May 2018
MO024-003----:
Situated on a slight rise between drumlins, it is not depicted on any OS map. This is a court-tomb with a slightly curved gallery (L c. 5m; Wth 1.4m) aligned roughly NW-SE. A single stone to the SE of the gallery is probably a court stone. A number of the stones are shattered.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 9 May 2018
MO024-027----:
Located just off the crest of a S-facing slope. A roughly trapezoidal grass-covered mound (L 31m; Wth 11.5m) with some scrub is aligned NE-SW. A series of displaced flags at the NE end may represent the shallow court. Behind these are two subsidiary chambers opening to the NW and another opening to the SE. There are a number of set stones which appear to represent other chambers further SW, although no main gallery is evident. The surviving chambers are comparable to court-tomb subsidiary chambers.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore

MO025-005----:
The following description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Date of upload/revision: 17 July 2007
Remains of court-tomb consisting of mound (L 30m; Wth 14.5m) aligned NW-SE and narrowing to SE. Near NW are two jambs and side stone of gallery opening to N which is partly obscured by fence which crosses site form NW to SE. A set stone S of fence my indicate a continuation of structure.
MO025-021----:
Located towards the bottom of a W-facing slope and c. 2m out from a NW-SE field bank on the NE side. It is described in gothic lettering as the site of a ‘Druid’s Altar’ only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map. The OS Revision Name Book describes this as "A rude flag about 2.25 ft in breadth and 2.5 ft in height, and it is said to have stood over Tubber na Downey or Sunday well (as tradition says) before it (i.e. the well) moved by some spell to the south end of the townland where it still remains' (1857, Sheet 25D, p.9). The stone (L 1.16m; Wth 0.45m; H 0.5m) was parallel with the field bank. A private house was built on this plot c. 40m to the SE before 1995 (OSAP), but archaeological testing (10E0208) in the plot immediately to the SW produced no related material (McGonigle 2010, 2012).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 27 February 2018
Amended: 17 January 2020
MO025-022----:
Situated on a low-lying NW-SE spur. It is described in gothic lettering as ‘Cloghaphooka ‘ – Cloch an Phúca, the ghost’s stone – only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map. This ruined monument is represented by three set stones incorporated in a mound (L 4.5m; Wth 6m). One of these (dims c. 1.1m x c. 0.2m; H c. 1.4m) at the S is a tall gable-shaped stone, perhaps a back stone. Some 3m to the N are two stones, possibly jambstones (H c. 0.35; 0.45m). The area between these has been recently dug out. The remains are insufficient for a closer classification.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 27 February 2018
MO025-027----:
Situated on a rise on a NE-facing slope. It is described in gothic lettering only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map as ‘Minnavarmore’. In the folk tradition it is the burial place of a Scandinavian giant called Manowar, who came here to kill Fin McCool. Fearing the foreign visitor, Fin had himself disguised as a baby by his wife and bit Manowar on the finger when the latter attempted to tease him. As this was just the baby Manowar became afraid and attempted to leave but dropped dead mysteriously afterwards (Flanagan 1933; IFC, Schools MSS, (931), 184-88: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes). A single gallery (L 4.5m; Wth c. 1.7m) is aligned E-W with two jamb stones surviving at the E end. The interior is obscured by spoil.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 27 February 2018
MO026-009----:
Situated on a rise in a fairly low-lying landscape. A cairn (L c. 21m; Wth 11m) is aligned NNW-SSE. At N a sidestone supports a large displaced roof stone, perhaps representing a chamber opening to the N. Close to this, three set stones represent a subsidiary chamber opening to the W. The monument is unclassified, although it is likely to be either of the court-or portal-tomb classes.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 26 February 2018
MO027-049----:
Situated on a broad, low hill. It Is depicted faintly as an oval feature (max. dims c. 15m E-W; c. 8m N-S) described in gothic lettering as ‘Trein Mor’s Grave’ on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map. Trein Mór (the great strong one) was the grandfather of Fionn Mac Cumhaill, mythical leader of the Fianna, as recorded in the local folk lore (IFC Schools Ms, 939, 267; 940, 42: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes). The present landowner recalls that there was a grave here, 8ft by 5 ft (c. 2.4m x c. 1.5m), formed of stones set on edge. There is a scrub-covered area obscured by field stones against the field bank to the W.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 30 January 2018
MO027-057----:
Located on a rise in a slight NW-SE valley. It is recorded in the folk tradition (IFC, Schools’s MSS, 940, 41: https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes ) as a giant’s grave and while the name of the giant is not known, it does provide a sketch. This monument consists of a narrow gallery (L c. 4.5m; Wth 1.9m) aligned NE-SW and facing SW, but the back-stone is missing. It is defined by four or five side-stones flanked on either side by outer walling which extends 2m beyond the gallery to the SW. There is a marked decrease in the height of the orthostats from SW to NE. One roof-stone lies SE of the gallery. (de Valera and O' Nualláin 1982, 131)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Monaghan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1986). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
See the attached sketch from the Schools' Manuscripts
Revised by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 31 January 2018

It is described in gothic lettering as ‘Fin McCool’s Table’ on the 1834 edition of the OS 6-inch map, and the OS Memoirs record that 'it is said that there once was a cromlech and the pieces of rock of which it was composed were not long since destroyed for the purposes of being converted into lime in the kiln at the side of the cliff’ (RIA Box 49, Magheross Parish, p. 22a).
